title: Tortilla Chips 300g

drivers.name: Price increase to $3.97
drivers.evidence: Two prior weeks at $3.97 saw sales at 88% and 60% of baseline; noise-adjusted estimate x0.82

drivers.name: Supplier delivery warning
drivers.evidence: Planner note indicates supply risk; no past data, but credible as demand deterrent

adjustment.analysis: The baseline median is 124.1. The price is raised to $3.97 (+3.7%), which historically reduces demand. Past price spikes at $3.97 (2026-09-28, 2026-10-05) saw sales drop to 106 and 75—12% and 40% below baseline, respectively. The noise-adjusted effect of a $3.97 price is x0.82. A supplier delivery warning adds supply risk, lowering demand confidence. No events, promotions, or seasonal drivers. The uplift model suggests no change, but judgment overrides it. The price effect is strong and consistent, while the delivery note adds downside uncertainty.

brief:
PRODUCT: Tortilla Chips 300g | category Snacks | Store #12 (Austin, TX)
TARGET WEEK: 2026-11-30 to 2026-12-06 (8 weeks after the last week with sales data)

KNOWN PLAN FOR THE TARGET WEEK:
  events: none
  shelf price: 3.97 (+3.7% vs regular price 3.83)
  planner notes: Supplier warns of a short delivery

STATISTICAL BASELINE (exponential smoothing of recent sales; it ignores events, promotions and prices):
  median 124.1 | 5%-95%: 77.2 - 200.6 | 10%-90%: 88.7 - 170.3

In the evidence below, 'vs baseline' = actual units / what this same baseline predicted for that week.
It is the multiplier that would have been right, so it maps directly onto median_multiplier.
This product's ordinary weeks already swing about +/-29% around the baseline, so a past effect smaller than that, seen only a few times, is mostly noise. The
'noise-adjusted estimate' is the effect shrunk toward x1.0 for that noise and the number of sightings.
